title: One minute, in the car
summary: The coach puts the clipboard down for a week. The pouch travels: a slip is drawn at a red light or halfway up a hill, thirty seconds to think, one minute to talk, no table and no standing spot. Then argue whether the best fun is the kind that was hard while it was happening.
materials: the pouch, or any small bag, and a dozen blank slips
a one minute timer that somebody else holds
a car, a footpath, a queue, a hill: five different places, none of them a table

steps.title: The coach puts the clipboard down
steps.body:
For two weeks you have been in the corner: building somebody else's case file, running drills at them, playing the nastiest opponent you could invent. This week the corner is empty and it is your mouth again. That is deliberate, and so is how light this week is. It is the lightest week of the season in all three tracks, because the weekend is where the weight is.

The format is one you already own. A folded slip comes out of the pouch, you read it out loud, you get thirty seconds, then you talk for one whole minute. Point, reason, example, meaning: your four moves from last season, and they are not being retaught, only named, because you have them.

What is new is the room, and the room is that there is no room. No table. No spot on the carpet you always stand on. No warning. The pouch rides in the car door pocket all week, and a slip gets drawn where you happen to be: at a red light, halfway up a hill with your breath already short, third in a queue with strangers close enough to hear. Every one of those takes something away that you have been quietly leaning on. Speaking in a moving car with nobody looking at you is a strangely hard thing, because you get no faces back and you have to keep going anyway.

Two rules, both old. Silence beats um: when the thread goes, stop and count one, two, because a pause sounds like thinking from the outside and lasts no time at all to anybody but you. And laughing is allowed, stopping is not. If the slip is ridiculous, say so and keep going. If you contradict yourself halfway through, say that too and keep going. Sitting down at forty seconds is the only real way to lose here.

One note about the clock, so it does not get mixed up with the other one. A timer has lived in this house's debate rounds since last season and it lives here for the same reason it always did: a minute is the shape of the exercise. It has nothing to do with the clock that runs on Saturday, and the two of them are not the same kind of thing at all.

This week's question travels with the pouch: why do hard things feel good afterward? The lazy answer is because they are over. Get past that one in the first ten seconds and see what is underneath it. Some hard things feel good afterwards and some just feel horrible afterwards, and the interesting question is what tells them apart.

steps.title: The pouch rides in the car door
steps.body:
First, fill it, and you write every slip yourself. Twelve of them, folded, in the pouch by the end of the hour.

Four silly. The best seat in any car and why everybody else is wrong. A food that is pretending to be a different food.

Four about this summer, but not about how it is going. Things like: the thing I have changed my mind about since June, or what I would tell somebody who is about to start learning a second language.

And four that you cannot possibly answer in a minute. Why is anything fair. What is a person for. Those ones are not unfair slips, they are the good ones, because with a minute you cannot cover the ground and you are forced to do the thing a speaker actually does, which is choose one corner of it and go there properly.

You write all twelve, which means you cannot know which one is coming, only that it was yours.

Then the pouch leaves the house. Five draws across the week, in five different places, and not one of them at a table. Anybody holding the pouch may call one at any time. Each draw is the same: they hand it over, you read it out loud, thirty seconds of thinking with nothing written down, then the minute.

After each minute, whoever drew it says exactly two things and then stops talking: one thing that worked, one thing to change next time. No rescuing you mid-minute, however long the pause gets. That rule is theirs to keep and it is harder for them than for you.

One of the five has to be while walking, ideally uphill. Notice what your voice does when your breath is not under your control. Speakers spend years learning to hear that, and you can get it for free on one hill.
checklist: Twelve slips are folded in the pouch and I wrote every one of them myself
Five minutes were delivered in five different places, and none of them was at a table
One of the five was while walking, and I said afterwards what my voice did differently
Nothing was written down in any of the thirty seconds of thinking time
After each minute the person who drew the slip said one thing that worked and one thing to change, and nothing else

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record at least two of the five impromptu minutes, and one of the two has to be the walking one, with the timer audible or in shot. Do not stop recording during a pause, because the pause is part of what you are learning to hear. Then, in the same recording and sitting still this time, answer this week's question in your own words: why do hard things feel good afterward? Name one hard thing that felt good afterwards and one that did not, and say what you think the difference between them actually was.
